section_summary: This section consists of clippings from the English-language press in Tokyo (primarily The Japan Advertiser, including translations of editorials from the Fukuoka Nichi-Nichi, Tokyo Nichi-Nichi, and Hochi) covering Japanese Diet sessions, political commentary, and official reports between January 31 and February 4, 1934. Parliamentary interpellations focus heavily on foreign affairs—including the Indo-Japanese trade pact, Soviet-Japanese border and fishery disputes, relations with the United States and Great Britain, and upcoming naval ratio negotiations—alongside sharp debates over military interference in civilian governance and the administrative status of Manchukuo. The materials also detail domestic political party maneuvers against the non-party Saito Cabinet, legislative stagnation, industrial controversies surrounding the Japan Iron Foundry merger and Teikoku Rayon stock transactions, and official government statistics on salaries, banking, foreign currency assets, and ministerial secret funds.

subfiles.about: A report on Lower House Budget Committee interpellations regarding the Indo-Japanese trade pact, Soviet-Manchukuo border defense, China policy, and environmental damage from the Ashio copper mine.
subfiles.summary: At a meeting of the Lower House budget committee, interpellators including Ryuji Nagashima and Mitsugu Tanaka subjected the Government to questioning over foreign policy and economic issues. Nagashima and Tanaka criticized the outcome of the Indo-Japanese commercial negotiations and pressed Foreign Minister Koki Hirota and War Minister Senjuro Hayashi on tensions along the Soviet-Manchukuo frontier, with Hirota proposing demilitarization of the border and denying any immediate danger of conflict. Hirota and Commerce Minister Kumakichi Nakajima defended trade policy and quota agreements with India, while Admiral Mineo Osumi declined to disclose discussions from Five Ministers conferences. The session concluded with questions from Hikosaburo Kurihara concerning arsenic pollution from the Ashio copper mine contaminating the Watarase River, to which Parliamentary Vice-Minister of Home Affairs Takao Saito answered detailing annual preventive expenditures.
subfiles.title: Indian Trade Pact Denounced in Diet as Blow to Japan

subfiles.about: An editorial calling upon the Ministry of Home Affairs to suppress militaristic publications and rightist movements with the same vigor applied to communist activities.
subfiles.from: Fukuoka Nichi Nichi / The Japan Advertiser
subfiles.summary: The Fukuoka Nichi Nichi comments favorably on the decision of the Ministry of Home Affairs to restrict publications that stimulate warlike sentiment and popular misconceptions of impending conflict. However, the paper severely reproaches the Home Office for long tolerating chauvinistic propaganda, anti-foreign mass meetings, and rightist movements while ruthlessly suppressing communism. The editorial warns that unchecked nationalist agitation fosters reckless hostility toward the Soviet Union and the United States, gives rise abroad to damaging rumors of an impending Japanese dictatorship, and poses a grave constitutional threat to the Imperial system.
subfiles.title: Control Over Books

subfiles.about: A detailed report on Diet proceedings reviewing Soviet-Japanese relations, naval limitation treaties, South Seas mandates, northern fishery negotiations, and the Japan Iron Foundry merger.
subfiles.summary: In the House of Peers, former Foreign Minister Kenkichi Yoshizawa delivered a major speech arguing that no dispute between Japan and the Soviet Union warranted war and counseling against convening the 1935 naval parley without prior agreement. Foreign Minister Koki Hirota affirmed that Japan's mandate in the South Seas remained unaffected by its departure from the League of Nations and answered questions from Seiichi Aoki regarding Soviet fishery rights and state auction systems. In both houses, members debated the contentious amalgamation creating the Japan Iron Foundry Company, with Commerce Minister Kumakichi Nakajima defending asset evaluations against critical scrutiny by Mitsunoshin Kamiyama. Additional questions addressed agricultural relief bounties, rural land taxation, and freight rate reductions by Railway Minister Chuzo Mitsuchi.
subfiles.title: Diet Speaker Says Russia, Japan Have No Real War Cause

subfiles.about: An official statistical release by the Navy Ministry comparing Japanese and American naval strength and treaty ratios projected to the end of 1936.
subfiles.summary: In response to a Diet interpellation by Seiyukai member Shinya Uchida, the Navy Ministry published comparative tables projecting Japanese and United States naval holdings at the end of 1936 under current treaty limits. The figures show an aggregate ratio of 0.68 to 1.00 in favor of the United States if over-age vessels are counted, but a ratio of 0.81 to 1.00 in favor of Japan among vessels within treaty age limits. Navy Minister Mineo Osumi emphasized that over-age American warships remain active in fleet training and possess undiminished combat efficiency. Detailed comparative breakdowns are provided across capital ships, aircraft carriers, cruisers, destroyers, and submarines.
subfiles.title: Naval Comparisons of U. S., Japan Given

subfiles.about: A report on Diet sessions questioning cabinet ministers over military political interference, defense reorganization, air force unification, and national expenditures.
subfiles.summary: Members of both Diet houses pressed the Government regarding military political activism and foreign policy alignment following Japan's diplomatic isolation after withdrawing from the League of Nations. Jinjiro Mizuno urged the creation of a unified defense ministry and coordinated air training, though Premier Makoto Saito and War Minister Senjuro Hayashi stated that distinct army and navy missions made formal amalgamation unfeasible. Hayashi and Navy Minister Mineo Osumi acknowledged that military personnel should refrain from unnecessary political public statements while defending informational remarks concerning national defense. The debate also covered rice control legislation, projected loan issuances, Manchurian budget appropriations, and Seiyukai member Eikichi Hikita's protest over the public adulation accorded to Konichi Nakaoka, the released assassin of former Premier Takashi Hara.
subfiles.title: Questioning in Diet Criticizes Defense and Foreign Policy

subfiles.about: A brief news item reporting Lower House member Eikichi Hikita's disclosure that retired generals had approached Premier Saito demanding his resignation.
subfiles.summary: In the House of Representatives, Seiyukai member Eikichi Hikita asserted that several retired generals had recently called upon Premier Makoto Saito and urged him to resign. The remark was made during a tense legislative climate marked by complaints against military political pronouncements and attacks against established political parties by the Meirinkai reserve officers' organization. Hikita warned the chamber that such actions by military officers threatened to alienate the armed forces from the civilian population.
subfiles.title: Diet Speaker Claims Saito Asked to Quit By Retired Generals

subfiles.about: An analytical article by Dr. S. Washio examining the political parties' coordinated parliamentary offensive against the military and the non-party Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Dr. S. Washio discusses the first two weeks of the Diet session, where the Seiyukai and Minseito formed a de facto united front to challenge military dominance and restore party prestige impaired since the May 15 Incident. Party leaders including Takejiro Tokonami, Chuji Machida, Yoshihisa Ando, Gotaro Ogawa, and Shinya Uchida attacked military pronouncements, political interference, and rising naval expenditures. However, fearing a severe public and extra-parliamentary military backlash, the parties curtailed their direct offensive against the military during the second week, shifting focus toward financial scandals involving Commerce Minister Kumakichi Nakajima, including Teikoku Rayon shares, Kobe Iron Works transactions, and the iron industry merger. Washio concludes that although the parties seek a return to party government, their deep-seated rivalry and reliance on Diet demonstrations will produce few tangible results beyond embarrassing the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.title: Diet Attack Against Military Aims at Restoring Party Rule

subfiles.about: An editorial examining why foreign powers, particularly the Soviet Union, have received Foreign Minister Hirota's cooperative diplomatic overtures with skepticism.
subfiles.summary: The Hochi assesses international reactions to Foreign Minister Koki Hirota's address to the Diet advocating international accommodation, contrasting it with Count Yasuya Uchida's former unyielding diplomacy. The editorial observes that while Britain and the United States expressed cautious favor, Soviet leaders including Joseph Stalin, Vyacheslav Molotov, and Karl Radek responded with open distrust and calls to reinforce Far Eastern defenses. The paper advises Japanese leaders not to pursue international accord with unseemly haste, cautioning that unilateral accommodation without genuine reciprocal understanding risks degenerating into a subservient foreign policy.
subfiles.title: Hirota Not Comprehended

subfiles.about: An editorial commending the constructive exchange between Kenkichi Yoshizawa and Foreign Minister Hirota in the House of Peers regarding diplomatic moderation.
subfiles.summary: The Nichi-Nichi expresses satisfaction with the interpellation conducted in the House of Peers by former Foreign Minister Kenkichi Yoshizawa and the responses delivered by Foreign Minister Koki Hirota. The paper supports Yoshizawa's arguments for an upward revision of naval ratios and adequate national defense while commending his insistence that diplomatic avenues be thoroughly explored to resolve differences with the Soviet Union and other powers. It endorses Hirota's efforts to calm public anxiety, deprecate sensationalist discussions of an inevitable 1935-1936 international crisis, and steer foreign policy by principles of justice and moderation.
subfiles.title: Yoshizawa Encourages Hirota

subfiles.about: A report on Lower House interpellations demanding reform of the Kwantung Army's multiple administrative offices and criticizing military political encroachment.
subfiles.summary: Minseito member Hideo Ikeda challenged the government in the Lower House over the concentration of power in Manchuria, where one general concurrently serves as Kwantung Governor-General, Kwantung Army Commander, and Ambassador to Manchukuo, also protesting the transfer of consular police functions to the military gendarmerie. War Minister Senjuro Hayashi admitted the plural-office system was anomalous in theory but insisted it remained indispensable under prevailing conditions. Seiyukai interpellator Chokichi Miyawaki expressed alarm over tendencies toward military dictatorship, prompting Hayashi to deny any military intention of seizing political control. Later sessions featured Naohiko Seki questioning administrative discipline, Overseas Minister Ryutaro Nagai defending South Manchuria Railway reorganization announcements, and the House of Peers passing the first reading of the Agricultural Warehouse Law.
subfiles.title: Need of Clarifying Japan's Position in Manchuria Pressed

subfiles.about: An editorial asserting Japan's right to demand naval armament equality and an upward revision of treaty ratios at the 1935 conference.
subfiles.summary: The Nichi-Nichi reviews statements by Foreign Minister Hirota and Navy Minister Osumi in the Diet and recalls proposals submitted by delegate Naotake Sato at Geneva in 1932 to argue that Japan must insist on equality in defensive armaments at the upcoming 1935 naval parley. The editorial argues that the Washington Naval Treaty was merely a temporary expedient whose restrictive ratios ignored national sovereignty and changes in the geopolitical landscape. It maintains that authentic disarmament must be voluntary and reciprocal, asserting that no coalition of powers possesses the moral or legal right to dictate inferior defense limitations to an independent nation.
subfiles.title: Japan to Ask Equality

subfiles.about: An editorial commending the Diet for restoring its public stature by addressing national issues with sobriety and dampening alarmism over an impending crisis.
subfiles.summary: The Hochi praises the Diet for rehabilitating parliamentary prestige through constructive questioning of government policy rather than petty party squabbling. The editorial specifically applauds legislators and ministers for dispelling the fatalistic belief that an unavoidable national crisis will culminate in 1935-1936, praising the straightforward explanations provided by Foreign Minister Hirota and War Minister Hayashi. While commending parliamentary inquiries into Baron Kumakichi Nakajima's handling of the iron foundry merger, the paper cautions against premature impeachment proceedings until all relevant facts are established.
subfiles.title: Diet Politics Picking Up

subfiles.about: An official compilation of government statistical reports submitted to the Diet budget committee detailing secret funds, official salaries, foreign securities, and bank deposits.
subfiles.summary: At the request of the plenary budget committee of the Diet, the Government presented detailed statistical data spanning administrative salaries, colonial banking, foreign securities, and ministerial secret funds. For the 1931-1932 fiscal year, official salaries totaled 169,058,000 yen with bonuses and solatiums amounting to 25,583,000 yen (15.1 percent). Secret funds allocated for 1934-1935 reached 13,814,800 yen across general and special accounts, with the War Ministry receiving the largest share of 7,334,405 yen primarily for Manchurian Incident operations. The report also tabulates banking deposits totaling 10,552,571,000 yen across Japanese prefectures, Formosa, and Karafuto, along with 703,070,000 yen in Japanese foreign currency securities and 358,974,000 yen in foreign securities held as of October 1, 1933.
subfiles.title: Government Gives Statistics to Diet

subfiles.about: A report on a statement by the Kokumin Domei condemning the Saito Government and majority parties for delaying essential agrarian and election reform legislation.
subfiles.summary: Leaders of Kenzo Adachi's Kokumin Domei gathered in a closed meeting at the Diet building to draft a public declaration criticizing the Saito Cabinet and its major party allies, the Seiyukai and Minseito. The party pointed out that with one-third of the Diet session already elapsed, the Government had failed to submit promised measures for farm relief, election law revision, and other critical reforms. Warning that such procrastination undermines public confidence in parliamentary governance, the statement accused the ministry of temporizing. The caucus also decided that Yojiro Matsutani would represent the party during the upcoming debate on the Peace Preservation Law revision bill.
subfiles.title: Ministry Criticized by Kokumin Domei
